To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

brain-damaged drivers are slower and less accurate on a car-following task than controls, but that the older drivers are not; the older drivers are slower than the controls and patients on a time estimation task; and the older drivers are more accurate than the patients, but not the controls, on a car-follow-ing task.

brain damage and aging affect the ability to process information and to respond to it, and that these abilities are not affected equally by the similarity of the laboratory task to the driving task, the type of task, and the type of response required.

(1) RT tasks that require a decision between two stimuli are sensitive to aging, but (2) tasks that require a response to only one stimulus (e.g., brake reaction time) are not sensitive to aging, and (3) RT tasks are more sensitive to brain damage than driving performance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between laboratory RT tasks and driving performance.
the effects of aging and of brain damage on driving performance.
the effects of age-related or brain-related changes in information processing on the perception-response capabilities of drivers and their relation to driving performance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
RTs are not good predictors of driving performance, and that RTs are sensitive to aging but insensitive to brain damage.
RT tasks can be useful to predict driving behavior only when the driving task is highly similar to the laboratory task.
RT tasks are useful predictors only for brain-damaged drivers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
brain-damaged drivers are impaired on tasks that are similar to real-life driving tasks and that this deficit may be related to the speed and accuracy of their responses to compound stimuli.

the effects of brain injury and aging on driving performance are not necessarily reflected in the effects on simple reaction time, and that driving performance is not necessarily reflected in simple reaction time.

the brain-damaged patients and the older subjects were slower and less responsive than controls on RT tasks, but only the patients showed a deterioration of driving accuracy with increasing task load.
The main takeaway from our work is that
brain damage, and to a lesser extent aging, affects the ability to process and respond to complex stimuli.
the effects of aging and brain damage on driving performance are not uniform across tasks and that the effects of brain injury on driving are not limited to the effects of injury on RTs.
the effects of brain injury and aging on driving performance are complex and that a single laboratory task cannot be used to assess driving ability.
